  "title": "DiagPRM: Stage-Level Diagnostic Reasoning Rewards for Code Repair Search",
  "core_problem": "Reward models for code repair agents operate at granularities that each miss critical information. Trajectory-level scorers (SWE-RM achieves 62–74.6% on SWE-bench Verified via best-of-32) provide a single holistic continuous [0,1] score for the entire multi-turn interaction but cannot localize which reasoning stage—localization, diagnosis, or patch design—caused failure, limiting their value for credit assignment and trajectory steering. Patch-level verifiers (R4P achieves 72.2% verification accuracy via reasoning about final patches) skip the diagnostic process entirely. Rubric-based critics (OpenHands Rubric-Supervised Critic achieves +15.9 best-of-N improvement on the rerankable subset via 25 rubric features) evaluate a mix of behavioral indicators and reasoning adequacy judgments—including features like insufficient_analysis, insufficient_debugging, and misunderstood_intention that assess whether the agent's reasoning was adequate—but these features are independent categorical indicators, not a causally linked decomposition: knowing that 'insufficient_debugging' and 'incomplete_implementation' both fired does not reveal whether the agent failed because it mislocalized the fault (causing downstream diagnosis and patch failure) or correctly localized but misdiagnosed the root cause. Step-level action-utility PRMs (SWE-Shepherd) attempt localized scoring but suffer fundamental credit assignment noise—actions that look locally useful may lead to dead ends, yielding 51% vs. 57% for greedy baselines. Prompt-based behavioral PRMs (SWE-PRM achieves 40→50.6% via course-correction) detect process inefficiencies like looping and drift but do not evaluate the logical soundness of diagnostic reasoning. Can we build a step-level PRM that scores reasoning quality along the causal diagnostic chain—localize → diagnose → patch—and use stage-level credit assignment to guide repair search and enable targeted resampling?",
  "opportunity": "Code repair follows a diagnostic reasoning structure (localize → diagnose → patch) where intermediate diagnostic claims make verifiable predictions checkable against test execution outcomes—a domain-specific advantage absent from code generation or general agent tasks. This creates three opportunities no existing system exploits simultaneously: (1) Causal stage decomposition enables localized credit assignment that trajectory-level scorers (SWE-RM) and independent feature indicators (OpenHands Critic) cannot provide—the three stages form a causal chain where localization quality constrains diagnosis quality, which constrains patch quality, so identifying the first failing stage localizes the root cause of trajectory failure and enables targeted resampling from that stage onward; (2) Reasoning quality at each stage is a property of the reasoning chain itself, not of future actions, making it a lower-variance scoring target than action utility (SWE-Shepherd), with a formal argument: Var(Q_reasoning|prefix) = 0 as Q depends only on observables, while Var(U_action|prefix) > 0 as U depends on stochastic future decisions; (3) Test execution outcomes serve as automatic validators for reasoning quality annotations during training—not as runtime input (addressing Haque et al.'s finding)—enabling training label quality verification that general-purpose reasoning evaluators (Agent-RRM) lack because they have no domain-specific ground truth. The distinction from the OpenHands Rubric-Supervised Critic requires nuance. The Critic's 25 rubric features are not all purely behavioral pattern detectors—features like insufficient_analysis (failed to examine existing materials), insufficient_debugging (avoided investigating failures), and misunderstood_intention (misinterpreted user's goal) genuinely assess reasoning adequacy. DiagPRM's contribution is orthogonal along a different axis: rather than evaluating 25 independent categorical indicators (each binary present/absent, producing a feature vector for quality prediction), DiagPRM decomposes reasoning into three causally linked cognitive stages and evaluates the logical soundness of reasoning at each stage—does the localization reasoning correctly connect evidence to fault location? does the diagnosis hypothesis explain the observed failure? does the fix rationale follow from the diagnosis? This causal decomposition provides three capabilities independent features cannot: (a) root-cause identification—knowing that the agent failed at the diagnosis stage (not localization) directs resampling to the right point; (b) targeted resampling—regenerating only from the failing stage rather than the full trajectory; (c) causal credit assignment—a bad patch score propagates credit to the diagnosis stage if the patch faithfully implements a flawed diagnosis, rather than penalizing the patch reasoning itself. While SWE-PRM pioneered PRMs for SWE agents, it uses prompt-based behavioral pattern detection (looping, drift, redundancy) without training—complementary to but distinct from trained reasoning quality evaluation. RGFL generates structured reasoning explanations for fault localization (85% Hit@1) and R4P reasons about patches, but neither trains a reward model for search guidance across the full diagnostic process. Agentic Rubrics (arXiv:2601.04171) generate repository-grounded checklists for execution-free patch verification (54.2% on SWE-bench Verified), but evaluate the output artifact (the patch) against external criteria rather than the reasoning process that produced it. CodeTracer performs post-hoc stage-level failure onset localization for debugging, but produces diagnostic labels for human consumption rather than reward scores for search guidance. ORPS demonstrates execution-grounded process rewards without a trained PRM, but requires execution at every search tree node and targets generation, not repair. RTMC (arXiv:2604.11037) achieves +3.2pp on SWE-bench Verified via rollout-tree-based step-level credit assignment, but operates at the action level without diagnostic stage structure. The gap—a trained step-level PRM that evaluates reasoning quality along the causal diagnostic chain (localize → diagnose → patch), using stage-level causal decomposition for credit assignment and targeted resampling, execution-free at inference—remains open.",
  "landscape": "SWE-PRM / When Agents Go Astray (arXiv:2509.02360, Sept 2025, IBM Research) is the first PRM applied to SWE agents: a prompt-based system using a taxonomy of behavioral inefficiencies (looping, drift, redundancy, specification violations) to course-correct agents at runtime, achieving 40.0→50.6% on SWE-bench Verified with closed-source PRMs. It evaluates behavioral process patterns—not diagnostic reasoning quality—and is not a trained model, instead invoking an off-the-shelf LLM with a sliding window of k=8 recent steps every 5 steps. SWE-RM (arXiv:2512.21919, Dec 2025, Qwen team) is the current strongest trained reward model for SWE agents: a 30B MoE model (3B active) trained on ~100K trajectories, producing continuous [0,1] scores via softmax of YES/NO token log-probabilities on whole trajectories, achieving 51.6→62.0% (Flash) and 67.0→74.6% (Max) on SWE-bench Verified via best-of-32 (RM@32), plus RL gains. It scores complete trajectories holistically but provides no step-level diagnostic feedback. Notably, its headline results use N=32 candidates; performance at smaller N is shown only in scaling curves without tabulated values, and stage-level credit assignment is most valuable precisely at small N where each candidate trajectory carries more weight. R4P/Patch Reasoner (arXiv:2510.22775, Oct 2025) frames patch verification as reasoning via group-wise RL, achieving 72.2% accuracy surpassing o3 and 50× faster than testing, but evaluates final patches, not the diagnostic process leading to them. OpenHands Rubric-Supervised Critic (arXiv:2603.03800, March 2026, UIUC/CMU) trains a lightweight 4B critic model using semi-supervised learning on real-world user-agent interactions, achieving Best@8 +15.9 over Random@8 on the rerankable subset of SWE-bench Verified and +17.7 with early stopping at 83% fewer attempts. It uses 25 rubric features plus 1 success prediction (26 total labels in the deployed model; 24 features in the published taxonomy). Crucially, these features are not all purely behavioral: while features like loop_behavior, file_management_errors, and improper_tool_use_or_setup are directly observable from action traces, features like insufficient_analysis (failed to examine existing materials before proceeding), insufficient_debugging (avoided investigating failures), misunderstood_intention (misinterpreted user's goal), and scope_creep (implemented unrequested features) require evaluating the adequacy and correctness of the agent's reasoning, not just its observable actions. The critical distinction from DiagPRM is structural, not categorical: the Critic evaluates 25 independent categorical indicators (each binary present/absent), producing a feature vector for quality prediction, while DiagPRM decomposes reasoning into three causally linked stages—localize → diagnose → patch—where identifying the first failing stage localizes the root cause and enables targeted resampling from that stage onward. Independent features tell you what went wrong (multiple possible labels); causal stages tell you where the reasoning chain broke and what to regenerate. Agentic Rubrics (arXiv:2601.04171, Jan 2026, Scale AI) creates repository-grounded rubric checklists for execution-free patch verification, achieving 54.2% on SWE-bench Verified with Qwen3-Coder-30B at Best@16. It evaluates the output artifact (the patch) against externally generated, instance-specific criteria rather than the reasoning process—complementary to but distinct from process-level reasoning evaluation. RGFL (arXiv:2601.18044, Jan 2026) generates structured per-candidate reasoning explanations for fault localization achieving 85% Hit@1 on SWE-bench Verified, but is a one-shot ranker—not a reward model—and covers only the localization stage, not diagnosis or patch design. Agent-RRM (arXiv:2601.22154, Jan 2026) produces decomposed trajectory judgments (reasoning trace + critique + holistic score) for general agent tasks (GAIA, WebWalkerQA) but is not specialized for code repair and lacks domain-specific ground truth for training label validation. ORPS (ICML 2025, arXiv:2412.15118) demonstrates that execution-grounded self-critique generates high-quality process rewards without trained PRMs (26.9% correctness gain), but requires execution at every search tree node—expensive and infeasible for large-repository repair—and targets code generation, not repair. SWE-Shepherd (arXiv:2604.10493, April 2026) introduces step-level action-utility PRMs for SWE agents but achieves only 51% vs. 57% greedy baseline on 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, confirming that action utility suffers credit assignment noise. SWE-TRACE (arXiv:2604.14820, April 2026) uses rubric-based PRMs with heuristic test-time scaling, achieving competitive results but relying on hand-designed rubric criteria rather than learned reasoning quality. RTMC (arXiv:2604.11037, April 2026) organizes group rollouts into a shared rollout tree for step-level credit assignment, achieving +3.2pp on SWE-bench Verified over GRPO, but operates at the action level without diagnostic stage structure and requires rollout-tree construction. CodeTracer (arXiv:2604.11641, April 2026) constructs hierarchical trace trees of agent execution and performs failure onset localization across five mechanical workflow stages (environment verification, dependency installation, inspection/debugging, patching, verification), achieving 46–48% F1 on CodeTraceBench (4,354 trajectories). It is a post-hoc diagnostic analysis tool producing failure labels for human debugging, not a reward model for search guidance; its five stages describe mechanical workflow phases, not cognitive diagnostic reasoning stages. TRAJEVAL (arXiv:2603.24631, March 2026) decomposes trajectories into mechanical search/read/edit stages for diagnostic evaluation (Pass@1 MAE 0.87–2.1%) but evaluates file/function retrieval precision, not cognitive reasoning quality. ExecVerify (arXiv:2603.11226, March 2026) trains execution-understanding rewards (next-statement/variable prediction) but targets execution trace comprehension, not diagnostic reasoning evaluation. Note on SWE-bench Verified: OpenAI announced in February 2026 that it would no longer evaluate on this benchmark, citing flawed test cases (59.4% of audited problems have tests that reject correct submissions) and data contamination (frontier models can reproduce verbatim gold patches from task IDs alone), and SOTA has reached 93.9%. SWE-bench Pro (1,865 multi-language tasks, contamination-resistant) is the recommended replacement. However, all existing reward model baselines (SWE-RM, SWE-Shepherd, SWE-TRACE, OpenHands Critic) report on Verified, making it the only benchmark enabling direct comparison with prior work. ThinkPRM (arXiv:2504.16828, April 2025) demonstrates data-efficient generative PRMs outperforming discriminative PRMs with 1% of process labels. AgentPRM (arXiv:2511.08325, ACM Web 2026) achieves 8× compute efficiency using TD-based estimation for agent PRMs. FunPRM (arXiv:2601.22249, Jan 2026) treats functions as PRM steps for code generation, achieving SOTA on LiveCodeBench. Agent-RLVR (arXiv:2506.11425, June 2025) trains SWE agents via guidance and environment rewards with patch-level reward model scoring.",
  "approach": "We define a 3-stage diagnostic reasoning taxonomy for code repair—localize (connect symptoms to fault location), diagnose (identify root cause), patch (design fix from diagnosis)—and extract stage boundaries from natural language repair trajectories using an LLM parser. These cognitive reasoning stages differ from CodeTracer's five mechanical workflow stages (env verification, dependency, inspection, patching, verification): our stages decompose the agent's reasoning process, not its tool-use workflow, enabling evaluation of logical soundness rather than execution correctness. They also differ structurally from the OpenHands Rubric-Supervised Critic's 25 rubric features: while we acknowledge that several Critic features (insufficient_analysis, insufficient_debugging, misunderstood_intention, scope_creep) assess reasoning adequacy rather than purely behavioral patterns, the critical structural difference is that the Critic's features are independent categorical indicators—each evaluated in isolation, producing a feature vector where knowing 'insufficient_debugging=True' and 'incomplete_implementation=True' does not reveal whether the agent mislocalized the fault (causing all downstream failure) or correctly localized but misdiagnosed the root cause. DiagPRM's three stages form a causal chain: localization quality constrains diagnosis quality, which constrains patch quality. This causal structure enables three capabilities impossible with independent features: (a) root-cause identification—pinpointing which cognitive stage first failed; (b) targeted resampling—regenerating only from the failing stage onward rather than the entire trajectory; (c) causal credit assignment—a bad patch receives appropriate credit when it faithfully implements a flawed diagnosis, rather than penalizing the patch reasoning itself. Using the publicly available SWE-smith 66K trajectory corpus (Kwai-Klear/SWE-smith-mini_swe_agent_plus-trajectories-66k), we annotate diagnostic reasoning quality at each stage via an LLM-judge (Claude/GPT-4o) that evaluates: (1) whether localization reasoning correctly connects error evidence to candidate locations, (2) whether the root cause hypothesis logically explains the observed failure, (3) whether the fix rationale follows from the diagnosis. We address the LLM-judge circularity concern through two mechanisms. First, we explicitly mine disagreement cases between reasoning quality and test outcomes as the most distinctive training signal: trajectories with sound reasoning but failed patches (correct diagnosis, implementation error) teach the PRM that the reasoning was good despite bad outcome, while trajectories with poor reasoning but passing patches (lucky guess, partial fix) teach it to penalize unsound reasoning despite success. These disagreement cases are exactly where DiagPRM provides information that outcome reward cannot. Second, the stage-level decomposition provides strictly more information than binary outcome: even when a trajectory fails, DiagPRM distinguishes 'good localization + bad diagnosis + bad patch' from 'bad localization + everything downstream wrong,' enabling localized credit assignment impossible with trajectory-level scoring. We acknowledge the LLM-judge reliability challenge highlighted by recent findings: arXiv:2604.27727 reports Cohen's kappa of only 0.1592 and Fleiss' kappa of 0.0696 for inter-LLM-judge agreement on coding evaluation. However, that study evaluates open-ended contest-style code co-creation quality using broad ordinal scales (algorithmic adequacy 1–5, robustness 1–5) with only 15 participants and 184 trajectories—a fundamentally different evaluation task. DiagPRM's evaluation criteria are substantially more structured: each stage has concrete, verifiable binary criteria (does the localization reasoning cite relevant error evidence from the stack trace? does the diagnosis hypothesis reference specific code behavior that explains the failing test? does the fix rationale address the diagnosed root cause rather than an unrelated issue?). Prior work on rubric-based LLM evaluation consistently finds that structured, criterion-separated rubrics yield higher inter-annotator agreement than holistic or broad ordinal assessments. Moreover, DiagPRM's criteria are grounded in observable artifacts (error messages, test outputs, code structure) rather than subjective quality judgments, further constraining annotator variance. The pilot study is explicitly designed to empirically test whether this structural advantage yields adequate agreement: if the 100-trajectory pilot reveals kappa below 0.4 on reasoning quality judgments, we will pivot to a hybrid approach combining high-agreement features (following the OpenHands Critic's demonstrated success with independent rubric features) with targeted causal stage-level reasoning quality criteria only for the most structured evaluation dimensions. We validate LLM-judge annotation quality through a pilot study on 100 trajectories (300 reasoning steps): three LLM judges (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) independently annotate reasoning quality, and we measure inter-model Cohen's kappa, correlation with test outcomes (expecting moderate ~0.4-0.6, not perfect, correlation—high correlation would indicate the PRM is a mere outcome proxy, while moderate correlation confirms it captures distinct information), and compare inter-annotator agreement for reasoning quality labels vs. action utility labels on the same trajectories. The 100-trajectory pilot provides sufficient statistical power to estimate kappa with a 95% confidence interval width of ±0.08–0.10 (per Sim & Wright 2005), adequate for distinguishing moderate from substantial agreement. We train DiagPRM as a lightweight LoRA-tuned classifier on Qwen3-8B (~15K annotated step-outcome pairs), following ThinkPRM's insight that small amounts of high-quality process labels suffice. We include a formal argument for the stability advantage: define reasoning quality Q(r_t) as a function of the reasoning chain r_t and observable evidence at step t. Q depends only on the trajectory prefix, so Var(Q|prefix) reflects only annotator noise. Action utility U(a_t) = E[R(τ)|prefix, a_t] depends on stochastic future actions, so Var(U|prefix) includes both annotator noise AND irreducible variance from unknown future decisions. Thus Var(Q|prefix) < Var(U|prefix) in expectation, explaining SWE-Shepherd's credit assignment failures. At inference, DiagPRM guides best-of-N selection and stage-level reranking. For SWE-bench Verified evaluation, we generate N∈{5,8,16} trajectories per instance on the same 100 instances used by SWE-Shepherd, using API-based agent trajectory generation (shifting cost from GPU to API budget). Reporting multiple N values is important because SWE-RM's headline results use N=32 (RM@32), while DiagPRM's stage-level credit assignment advantage is most pronounced at small N: with fewer candidates, correctly identifying which stage failed—and thus which trajectory has the soundest reasoning chain—provides more marginal value than holistic trajectory scoring. We additionally evaluate whether DiagPRM+SWE-RM combination outperforms either alone, testing whether stage-level causal reasoning scores and trajectory-level holistic scores provide complementary signal. We acknowledge that SWE-bench Verified faces well-documented concerns—OpenAI announced in February 2026 that it would no longer evaluate on this benchmark due to flawed test cases and data contamination—and SOTA has reached 93.9%, raising saturation questions. We retain Verified as our primary evaluation benchmark for three reasons: (a) all reward model baselines (SWE-RM, SWE-Shepherd, SWE-TRACE, OpenHands Critic) report on Verified, making it the only benchmark enabling direct comparison with prior work—switching to a different benchmark would prevent meaningful comparison; (b) our evaluation compares relative reranking effectiveness of different reward models on the same candidate trajectories, so any contamination affects the underlying agent equally across all reranking methods; (c) contamination primarily inflates absolute resolution rates rather than invalidating relative reward model comparisons, since the reward model itself is not contaminated on SWE-bench Verified tasks. The DebugBench evaluation (1,000 instances) provides complementary validation on a cleaner, non-deprecated benchmark. If timeline permits, we will additionally evaluate on a 50-instance subset of SWE-bench Pro to test generalization to the contamination-resistant, multi-language benchmark. We report bootstrap confidence intervals (1000 resamples) for all resolution rate comparisons and apply the paired bootstrap test for statistical significance of DiagPRM vs. each baseline. Given the 100-instance evaluation set and expected effect sizes of 3–8 percentage points, we acknowledge that small differences (≤3 pp) may not reach statistical significance (p<0.05). We therefore frame the quantitative contribution as twofold: (a) competitive or superior best-of-N selection accuracy vs. SWE-RM despite the 8B vs. 30B model size gap and the N=5 vs. N=32 setup difference, and (b) the qualitative capability of localized causal credit assignment enabling stage-level resampling—selectively regenerating only from the failing stage onward rather than the entire trajectory—which is impossible with both trajectory-level scorers and independent categorical feature indicators regardless of effect size. We evaluate against: (1) SWE-RM as primary baseline (trajectory-level scoring), testing both standalone comparison and DiagPRM+SWE-RM combination to demonstrate complementarity of stage-level causal and trajectory-level holistic signals; (2) OpenHands Rubric-Supervised Critic (independent categorical feature-based critic) to directly test whether causal stage decomposition of reasoning quality provides value beyond independent feature indicators—noting that the Critic's +15.9 improvement is reported on the rerankable subset, and we will use the same evaluation protocol for fair comparison; (3) SWE-PRM (prompt-based behavioral PRM) to demonstrate that trained reasoning quality evaluation provides value beyond behavioral pattern detection; (4) SWE-Shepherd (step-level action utility PRM); (5) SWE-TRACE (rubric PRM); (6) outcome-only best-of-N reranking; (7) random selection. We additionally evaluate on 1000 DebugBench instances (N=3, local model) across bug categories to test whether DiagPRM's per-stage scoring captures the category-dependent reasoning quality variation documented in DebugBench. We differentiate from the OpenHands Rubric-Supervised Critic not by claiming a clean behavioral/cognitive binary but by identifying the structural difference: its 25 features are independent categorical indicators evaluated in isolation, while DiagPRM's three stages form a causal chain enabling root-cause identification, targeted resampling, and causal credit assignment—capabilities that independent features, even those assessing reasoning adequacy, cannot provide; from Agentic Rubrics (arXiv:2601.04171) by noting it evaluates the output artifact (the patch) against repository-grounded checklists rather than the reasoning process that produced the patch—complementary to process-level evaluation since a patch passing all rubric criteria could still emerge from unsound reasoning (lucky convergence) while a failing patch could result from sound reasoning with an implementation error; from SWE-PRM by noting it is prompt-based behavioral monitoring (detecting looping, drift, redundancy) without training, complementary to but distinct from trained cognitive reasoning quality evaluation—SWE-PRM monitors whether the agent is working efficiently, DiagPRM evaluates whether the agent is reasoning correctly; from R4P by noting it evaluates final patches—orthogonal to diagnostic process evaluation, since a good patch can emerge from bad reasoning (lucky guess) and a bad patch from good reasoning (correct diagnosis, implementation error); from CodeTracer by noting it is a post-hoc diagnostic tool producing failure labels for human debugging across mechanical workflow stages, while DiagPRM produces per-stage reward scores across cognitive reasoning stages for automated search guidance and RL training; from RTMC by noting it achieves step-level credit assignment via rollout trees at the action level without diagnostic stage structure, requiring multiple rollouts per step, while DiagPRM provides stage-level credit via a single trained forward pass along the diagnostic causal chain; from RGFL by noting it is a one-shot localization ranker that cannot guide multi-candidate search or serve as RL reward; from Agent-RRM by noting its general-purpose design lacks code repair's verifiable intermediate claims for training label validation; and from ORPS by noting it requires execution at every search node while DiagPRM is execution-free at inference.",
